{{Short description|R-matrix}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''[[Brownian motion]] and the [[Riemann zeta function]]''' are two central objects of study in mathematics originating from different fields - [[probability theory]] and [[analytic number theory]] - that have mathematical connections between them. The relationships between [[stochastic process]]es derived from the Brownian motion and the Riemann zeta function show in a sense intuitively the stochastic behaviour underlying the Riemann zeta function. A representation of the Riemann zeta function in terms of stochastic processes is called a stochastic representation.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |author=[[David Williams (mathematician)|David Williams]] |title=Brownian motion and the Riemann zeta-function |encyclopedia = Disorder in Physical Systems: A Volume in Honour of John M. Hammersley | publisher=Oxford University Press |location=New York |date=1990 |pages=361–372 |url=https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~grg/books/hammfest/22-dw.pdf |isbn=0198532156}}</ref><ref name="MansuyYor"/>

==Brownian Motion and the Riemann Zeta Function==
Let <math>\zeta(s)</math> denote the Riemann zeta function and <math>\Gamma</math> the [[gamma function]], then the [[Riemann xi function]] is defined as
:<math> \xi(s) := \frac{1}{2}s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(\tfrac{1}{2}s)\zeta(s)</math>
satisfying the functional equation
:<math>\xi(s)=\xi(1-s),\quad \forall s\in \mathbb{C}.</math>

It turns out that <math>2\xi(s)</math> describes the moments of a probability distribution <math>\mu</math><ref name="MansuyYor">{{cite book |author=Roger Mansuy |author2=Marc Yor |title=Aspects of Brownian Motion |series=Universitext |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |year=2008 |pages=165–167 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-49966-4 |isbn=978-3-540-22347-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| author=Laurel Smith |author2=[[Persi Diaconis]] |title=Honest bernoulli excursions |journal=Journal of Applied Probability |date=1988 |volume=25 |number=3 | pages=464–477 |doi=10.2307/3213976 |jstor=3213976 }}</ref>

:<math>2\xi(s)=\mathbb{E}[X^s]=\int_{0}^{\infty} x^s d\mu(x),\quad \forall s\in\mathbb{C}</math>
===Brownian Bridge and Riemann Zeta Function===
In 1987 [[Marc Yor]] and [[Philippe Biane]] proved that the random variable defined as the difference between the maximum and minimum of a [[Brownian bridge]] <math>(b_s)_{0\leq s\leq 1}</math> describes the same distribution. A Brownian bridge is a one-dimensional Brownian motion <math>(W_t)_{0\leq t\leq 1}</math> conditioned on <math>W_0=W_1=0</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Philippe Biane |author2=Marc Yor |title=Valeurs principales associées aux temps locaux browniens |journal=Bulletin des Sciences Mathématiques |volume=111 |year=1987 |pages=23–101 |language=fr}}</ref> They showed that
:<math>X=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(\max\limits_{0\leq s \leq 1} b_s-\min\limits_{0\leq s \leq 1} b_s\right)</math>
is a solution for the moment equation
:<math>2\xi(s)=\mathbb{E}[X^s]</math>
However, this is not the only process related to this distribution, for example the [[Bessel process]] also gives rise to random variables with the same distribution.

===Bessel process and Riemann Zeta Function===
A [[Bessel process]] <math>\operatorname{Bes}(d)</math> of order <math>d</math> is the Euclidean norm of a <math>d</math>-dimensional Brownian motion. The <math>\operatorname{Bes}(3)</math> process is defined as
:<math>R_t:=\sqrt{\left(W_t^{(1)}\right)^2+\left(W_t^{(2)}\right)^2+\left(W_t^{(3)}\right)^2}.</math>
where <math>W_t=(W_t^{(1)},W_t^{(2)},W_t^{(3)})</math> is a <math>3</math>-dimensional Brownian motion.

Define the hitting time <math>T_1:=\inf\{t\geq 0\colon R_t=1\}</math> and let <math>\tilde{T_1}</math> be an independent hitting time of another <math>\operatorname{Bes}(3)</math> process. Define the random variable
:<math>N=\frac{\pi}{2}\left(T_1+\tilde{T_1}\right),</math>

then we have
:<math>2\xi(2s)=\mathbb{E}[N^s].</math><ref name="BPY">{{cite journal |author=Philippe Biane |author2=Jim Pitman |author3=Marc Yor |title=Probability laws related to the Jacobi theta and Riemann zeta function and Brownian excursions |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |series=New Series |volume=38 |year=2001 |issue=4 |pages=435–465 |doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-01-00912-0 |arxiv=math/9912170}}</ref><ref name="MansuyYor" />

===Distribution===
Let <math>\varphi</math> be the Radon–Nikodym density of the distribution <math>\mu</math>, then the density satisfies the equation<ref name="MansuyYor" />

:<math>\varphi(t)=2t \Theta''(t) + 3\Theta'(t)</math>
for the theta function<ref name="MansuyYor" />
:<math>\Theta(t)=\sum\limits_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\pi n^2t}.</math>
An alternative parametrization <math>G(y):=\Theta(y^2)</math> yields<ref name="BPY" />
:<math>h(y)=2y G'(y)+y^2G''(y).</math>
with explicit form
:<math>h(y)=4y^2\sum\limits_{n=1}^{\infty}\pi(2\pi n^4 y^2 - 3n^2)e^{-\pi n^2 y^2}</math>
where <math>h(y)=2y\varphi(y^2)</math> and
:<math>2\xi(s)=\int_0^{\infty} y^{s-1}h(y)dy.</math>
